title: A bus read: where, who, and when
scope: Authored study lesson using original ECE224 Part Va source diagrams. Numerical timing windows are separately labelled original examples, not device specifications. Source images stay local.

beats.title: Who is allowed to speak?

practice.question: For a memory read, who drives the address and who drives the returned data?
practice.answer: The master drives the address; the selected memory drives the returned data.

beats.text: Our first model had just two boxes, but your course diagram connects several devices to the same wires. This is the original diagram from page five, with its labels and connections preserved. Start with the red address line, and follow it from the processor toward the address decoders. The master supplies an address; the connected slaves decide whether that address selects them. A connection to a wire does not give every device permission to drive it at once. In the read we are studying, the selected slave drives the blue data wires and the master receives their value. Now imagine reversing the transfer to a write. The master supplies the data, and the selected slave receives it, even though the physical data connections remain the same. That is why a data bus can be bidirectional without all devices transmitting simultaneously. Control is more varied: the diagram explicitly allows both sending and receiving control signals. Notice the final interface, which includes direct memory access, or D M A. The course identifies it as both a possible master and a slave; its role depends on the transaction. Before this explanation begins, arbitration has already selected the master for this transfer. We are not claiming that a second master can seize the bus halfway through it. Pause and predict: for a read from memory, which device drives the address, and which drives the returned data? The master drives the address; the selected memory drives the returned data. Keep that ownership question beside our earlier distinction between where and what.

beats.title: Read the clock as a shared ruler

practice.question: Which clock edge completes the ideal read at the master?
practice.answer: The final positive edge, when the master stores data in its MDR.

beats.text: Now replace our generic handshake with the specific ideal synchronous read shown on page thirteen. The original slide is our evidence; the moving outlines are only a reading guide. Read time from left to right, and use the clock edges as shared vertical reference points. At the first positive edge, marked one, the master sets the address and the read or write signal. In this course diagram, a high read or write signal means a read. The address band becomes valid, but the data band has not yet become the valid answer. Follow the middle vertical guide to the negative clock edge, marked two. Here the slave decodes the address and control, then puts the data on the bus in this idealized sequence. Continue to the next positive edge, marked three. That is when the master stores the data in its memory data register. The address and data are drawn as bands because each stands for several wires, not a single binary signal. The band labelled valid data identifies a time interval; it does not mean that every bit is a one. A numerical value such as forty two can contain both zeros and ones while remaining valid throughout that interval. Ask yourself which edge completes the read at the master. It is the final positive edge where storage occurs, not the earlier edge where the address first appears. These are the rules of the displayed course example, not a universal rule for every synchronous interface. Next we will keep this sequence but stop pretending that signals arrive everywhere instantly.

beats.title: One wire, different arrival times
beats.text: The detailed diagram on page nineteen separates a signal at the master from the same signal at the slave. This duplication is essential: a shared connection still takes time to carry a change between its endpoints. Begin at the positive clock edge and compare the two address rows. The master side becomes stable first, after the driver's propagation delay. The slave side becomes stable later, after the additional bus propagation delay. A receiver cannot act on the new address merely because the sender has already started driving it. The original diagram shows a sloped transition and a stable band, rather than an exact instantaneous jump at both ends. Those transition regions remind us that arrival and removal times can vary. Now move to page twenty two and trace the return path. After the negative edge, the slave selects a register and accesses its contents. Its internal Data Valid signal becomes active before the returned data is stable at the master. The data must still travel through the slave's driver and across the bus. Follow the blue data bands: valid at the slave is an earlier event than valid at the master. Our sampling decision must use the data at the receiving master, not the more optimistic time at the producing slave. This is why adding a device access time alone can give the wrong timing answer. There are several stages in the path, and the original annotations name each stage. Pause here and point to the receiving endpoint before writing an inequality. The location of a timing requirement matters just as much as the number attached to it.

beats.title: A sampling edge has two sides
beats.text: Page twenty two requires the returned data to be stable before the receiving clock edge. Page twenty four adds a different requirement: it must remain stable after that edge for the required hold time. Let us make both requirements visible with a separate numerical example, not a set of specifications taken from the slides. Put the sampling edge at ten nanoseconds, with a setup time of two nanoseconds and a hold time of one nanosecond. The required stable window therefore begins at eight and ends at eleven nanoseconds. Suppose data becomes stable at six and does not change again until twelve. Draw that actual interval underneath the required interval, on exactly the same time scale. Its left endpoint is two nanoseconds earlier than the setup deadline, giving two nanoseconds of setup margin. Its right endpoint is one nanosecond later than the hold boundary, giving one nanosecond of hold margin. Both conditions pass in this bounded timing example. Now move only the arrival to eight and a half nanoseconds. Even though the value exists before the clock edge at ten, it misses the setup deadline by half a nanosecond. Move the arrival back to six, then move the next change to ten and a half. Setup passes, but hold fails by half a nanosecond. These are separate failure modes; moving one endpoint does not repair the other. The arithmetic checks interval containment at the receiving register. It does not simulate an analog waveform or prove that a particular physical circuit meets its specifications.

beats.title: Four edges form an agreement

practice.question: What permits the slave to release read data in the fully interlocked sequence?
practice.answer: The slave observes Master-Ready becoming inactive after the master stored the data, then completes release.

beats.text: A synchronous transfer agrees on clock edges in advance, but the course also shows a fully interlocked asynchronous alternative. On page thirty four, there is no shared clock trace; Master Ready and Slave Ready coordinate the read. We will follow only the first transaction on this slide, the read on the left. At event one, the master asserts Master Ready and supplies the read control and address. At event two, the selected slave supplies the data and asserts Slave Ready. The master then stores the returned data, deasserts Master Ready, and removes its address and control at event three in this ideal diagram. Finally, at event four, the slave deasserts Slave Ready and removes the data. Switch to page thirty five: the original arrows make the causal chain explicit. The first ready edge prompts the second; the second prompts the third; the third prompts the fourth. Think of the return to inactive as part of completing the conversation, not an irrelevant tail after the interesting number arrived. The second transaction drawn on the slide is a write and has different data ownership. We are deliberately keeping our highlight on the first read so that these two cases are not mixed together. Pause and predict which side can release its read data immediately after the master has sampled, under this fully interlocked sequence. The slave observes the master's acknowledgement through Master Ready becoming inactive, then completes its release. This agreement permits different transaction durations, but it still requires the signal ordering and timing constraints of the implementation. Asynchronous does not mean that propagation delay or stable-data requirements disappear.

beats.title: Ready also has to travel
beats.text: The ideal handshake hides the same physical issue as the ideal clocked transfer: an edge is not observed everywhere at once. Page thirty seven draws Master Ready separately at the master and at the slave. Follow the address to the slave first, then follow Master Ready to that same endpoint. The course requires the master to delay its ready indication so that the slave sees a stable address before it acts on that indication. Merely drawing two outgoing edges together at the sender would not establish their arrival order at the receiver. Page thirty eight follows the other direction. Slave Ready must travel back to the master, and the master also needs the returned data to be stable before storing it. The detailed design includes waiting and storage time rather than treating a ready edge as instantaneous permission everywhere. After storing the data, the master deasserts Master Ready. It delays removal of the address and control so that the slave sees the inactive ready signal before those selections can change. This ordering protects the identity of the transaction while its completion travels through the system. Page forty highlights the hold requirement at the receiving master after storage. The fully interlocked protocol controls release through acknowledgement, but the actual delays must still leave data valid for long enough. You do not need to redraw this crowded diagram from memory to study it. Keep the original, isolate one endpoint, and follow one causal path at a time. If a formula or label cannot be read reliably from extraction, return to the original image instead of inventing the missing symbols. The same approach works for other dense technical diagrams: preserve the evidence and animate the attention.

beats.title: Predict, then explain

practice.question: Address 16 is driven, but the wires show 19. Is 19 already the accepted answer?
practice.answer: No. The present bus value may be old; the receiving-side valid sampling condition has not been established.

practice.question: Sample at 10 ns, setup 2, hold 1. Does actual validity [7, 11.5] ns pass?
practice.answer: Yes. It covers [8, 11] ns, with 1 ns setup margin and 0.5 ns hold margin.

practice.question: The master stored data and lowered Master-Ready. What completes the read?
practice.answer: The slave observes the acknowledgement, lowers Slave-Ready and releases the data.

beats.text: Let us finish with three predictions, using the same distinctions throughout the lesson. First, a processor drives address sixteen while a data wire still carries nineteen. Without a valid sampling condition, can we conclude that nineteen is the value stored at address sixteen? Pause and give a reason before revealing the answer. No: the address identifies the requested location, but an old value on the data wires is not yet an accepted answer. Second, return to our numerical register example: sampling at ten, setup time two, and hold time one nanosecond. If the data is stable from seven until eleven and a half, does it contain the entire required stable window? The required window is eight through eleven, so it passes both conditions in this simplified example. Its setup margin is one nanosecond, and its hold margin is half a nanosecond. Third, in the fully interlocked read, what happens after the master stores the data and lowers Master Ready? The slave observes that acknowledgement, then lowers Slave Ready and releases the returned data, completing the four-event sequence. A correct answer should identify who acts, what that action means, and which earlier event permits it. For a new question during this lesson, pause on the relevant scene and attach the source or selected object so that the tutor has the actual context. Save a confusing moment for later, then try explaining it without replaying the answer immediately. The compact checklist is where, who, and when: selected address, permitted driver, and receiving-side validity. Keep the original evidence beside each explanation, and keep a calculated teaching example distinct from a hardware simulation.
